author: Thomas C. Schelling
biz: Put your constraints in writing, where enquirers can see them

Schelling's lesson is that a visible constraint persuades better than a claim. This week publish, on the HomeownersLoan and Apply4Loan landing pages and in the opening WhatsApp message, the limits you have placed beyond your own reach: that you are a credit broker and not a lender, how any fee works and when it could apply, the hour after which nobody is ever telephoned, and how quickly an enquirer will hear whether you can help. Nothing about guaranteed approval or rates. Measure enquiry to first contact time, drop-off after the first call, and complaints.
Replace we will be in touch with a focal point

Coordination fails without a salient marker, so stop issuing vague callback promises. This week every adviser agrees one named time and one channel with the client and confirms it in writing: I will ring at six this evening and send a WhatsApp message if you do not answer. For Debt Support Direct clients in distress, make the pause the default: no decision on the first call, written information to read, a fixed follow-up date. Measure answered callback rate, kept appointment rate, vulnerability flags recorded, and how many clients take the pause.

b: Thomas Crombie Schelling was born in Oakland, California, on the fourteenth of April 1921, into a family whose business was the management of force. His father was a naval officer, and in time so was his elder brother. Navy pay was steady pay, and when the Depression came through America the Schellings felt it rather less than their neighbours did. He grew up with a sense absorbed rather than taught: that armed men spend almost all of their lives not fighting.

His mother had graduate degrees and had taught before she stopped to raise three children. By his own later account she said to him one day, Tommy, it grieves me that you do not get better grades. It was a reproach from someone whose good opinion he wanted, and he began bringing home top marks. He would spend the next seventy years on exactly that puzzle: why some kinds of pressure move people and other kinds do not.

He finished school in San Diego and went north to Berkeley in 1939 to read economics. In 1940 he took himself off to Chile, where, by his own account, he worked as a night watchman at the American Embassy and then as assistant to an agent of the Federal Bureau of Investigation. When war came he tried to follow his father and his brother into the Navy, and a stomach ulcer kept him out.

So the son and brother of naval officers sat out the largest war in history in a library at Berkeley, taking his degree in 1944. The war he was not allowed to fight became the subject he could never leave alone.
ch.cap: A boy in a naval family on the Pacific coast
ch.h: A naval family and a mother's reproach

b: After the war he went to Washington and the Bureau of the Budget, and then, in 1948, into the great project of the age. The Marshall Plan was pushing American money into a ruined Europe, and it needed people who could read a table of national accounts and also sit in a room full of ministers. Schelling did both. He was posted to Copenhagen, to interpret economic statistics, and then to the Paris office under Averell Harriman.

He was in his late twenties, in rooms where grown countries bargained over coal and currency and wheat. There he noticed something the economics of the day had no language for. The negotiator who won was very often not the one with the strongest hand or the better argument. It was the one who could not move. A man who could say, truthfully, that his parliament would never ratify a penny more had the advantage over a man who was free to be generous.

Freedom, at a bargaining table, was a liability. The ability to give way was the very thing the other side was counting on. This is the thought everything else in his life grew out of, and he found it in a corridor rather than a seminar.

He was writing a doctorate at night through all of it. Harvard awarded it in 1951, and from 1951 to 1953 he worked at the White House and in the Executive Office of the President. He had watched how states actually talk to one another long before he wrote a word about it.
ch.cap: Learning that the man who cannot move wins
ch.h: Copenhagen, Paris, and the use of a tied hand

b: In 1953 he left government for Yale as an associate professor, and in 1956 published the paper that announced him. It was called An Essay on Bargaining, and the heading of its first section states the programme of his whole life: Bargaining Power, the Power to Bind Oneself.

The examples are what people remember, because they are funny and impossible to forget. If a man knocks at a door and says that he will stab himself on the porch unless given ten dollars, Schelling wrote, then he is more likely to get the ten dollars if his eyes are bloodshot. The threat is absurd. Its entire force comes from the possibility that the man is not in command of himself, and so cannot be reasoned out of it.

Or take the agent sent to negotiate with no authority to concede. He is weaker than his opponent in every respect that seems to matter, and that is exactly why he wins. In bargaining, Schelling wrote, weakness is often strength, freedom may be freedom to capitulate, and to burn bridges behind one may suffice to undo an opponent.

The insight runs against every instinct we have. We prize options and take care never to paint ourselves into a corner. Schelling's claim is that the corner is the weapon. A commitment you genuinely cannot escape hands the whole problem to the other side, since your own retreat has been made impossible and they must now decide whether to live with your terms.
The commitment must also be visible and believed: a promise you could quietly break on a Tuesday is worth nothing.

b: In 1956 he became an adjunct fellow of the RAND Corporation in Santa Monica, the institution the American air force had built to think the unthinkable, and spent the year from 1958 to 1959 there full time. In 1958 Harvard made him professor of economics. The seminar and the war room ran side by side in his life for more than a decade.
Out of journal articles written between 1957 and 1960 he assembled The Strategy of Conflict, published in 1960. It is usually filed under game theory. It is better read as a quarrel with it.

Formal game theory was then in love with the zero sum game, the clean case in which whatever one side gains the other must lose. Schelling thought this the least interesting kind of conflict and almost never the real one. Nearly every serious confrontation, he argued, is mixed motive. Two drivers racing for the same gap both want to get through first and both very much want to avoid the crash.

Once you see conflict that way, the central question changes. It is no longer how do I win. It is how do we reach any outcome at all, given that we are enemies with something in common. The answers turn out to be about promises, threats, deadlines, signals and trust between parties who do not trust each other. Morton Kaplan called the book a landmark in the literature in 1961, and a generation of strategists read it as a manual.
ch.h: RAND, and a quarrel with game theory

b: One of the book's experiments needed no equipment whatever. He put a problem to students. You and a stranger must meet in New York tomorrow. You cannot communicate, no place and no time has been named, and you get one attempt. Where do you go, and when?

There is no logical answer. There are many thousands of places. Yet the students did not scatter. A clear majority chose the information booth at Grand Central Station, at noon. Noon is not a better hour than eleven. It is simply the obvious one, and its obviousness was the whole of its value.

Schelling called these focal points. When people must coordinate and cannot talk, they reach for whatever is salient, prominent, conspicuous, whatever each can expect the other to notice. The clue need not be fair, or sensible, or efficient. It need only be mutually obvious. A round number. A river. A line already drawn on a map.

This explained a good deal that had looked inexplicable. Wars observe limits nobody has agreed to. Armies decline to use gas, because a limit that stands out is one both sides can hold to without appearing to concede.
The practical lesson is cheap and almost universally ignored. If you need people to act in concert and cannot brief every one of them, do not issue a rule. Give them something impossible to miss.
ch.h: Where will you meet in New York?

b: Then he turned the apparatus on the hardest problem of the age. American policy rested on a promise that an attack on Western Europe would be answered with nuclear weapons. Schelling saw the hole in it. West Berlin was militarily indefensible, and few in Moscow or Washington truly believed an American president would begin the end of the world over a place he could not hold.

A threat you would be insane to carry out is not a threat. If you cannot credibly promise to do something terrible, you can credibly arrange matters so that the terrible thing might happen anyway, and not entirely by your choosing. He called it the threat that leaves something to chance.

You do not say you will certainly retaliate. You place forces where a local commander may have to act, keep weapons forward, let a crisis acquire a momentum of its own, and make plain that once it starts neither of you may be able to stop it. The other side is then deterred not by your resolve, which it doubts, but by a risk it cannot control either. Brinkmanship, properly understood, is not bluffing. It is the deliberate manufacture of a danger you share.

From 1961 he did what few academics manage, which was to install his own idea inside a government. With a colleague he designed political war games played over three days at Camp David, the first from the eighth to the eleventh of September 1961, with Berlin as the scenario. The most senior player was the Attorney General, Robert Kennedy. The series ran some twenty five months, and when the last game finished, on Halloween 1963, he proposed turning the same method on desegregation.
ch.cap: Making the danger shared rather than chosen

b: In September 1960 the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists carried a short piece of his called Meteors, Mischief, and War, about the ways a war might begin that nobody had chosen. In it he discussed a novel, Red Alert, by the British writer Peter George, in which an American general dispatches his bombers on his own authority.

Stanley Kubrick read the article. Conversations followed between Kubrick, Schelling and George, and out of them came the 1964 film Doctor Strangelove, in which the machinery of deterrence functions exactly as designed and ends the world.

The same worry produced a duller and more useful result. Schelling credited Red Alert with making governments more aware of the value of being able to speak directly in a crisis. The Cuban missile crisis of October 1962, when messages between the capitals took hours, settled the argument. The Hot Line Agreement was signed in Geneva on the twentieth of June 1963 and the link began working on the thirtieth of August. Its first message was a test sentence typed entirely in capitals, because the machine had no lower case.

Several people had pressed for such a line, and Schelling was one voice among them rather than its inventor. But the reasoning was his. Where both sides share an interest in avoiding catastrophe, the ability to talk is not a courtesy. It is a weapon of peace.
ch.cap: Accidents, Kubrick, and a direct line

b: In 1966 he published Arms and Influence, where the argument stands with no padding. Diplomacy is bargaining, he wrote. And then the line everything turns on. The power to hurt is bargaining power. To exploit it is diplomacy, vicious diplomacy, but diplomacy.

The distinction he insisted on is between brute force and coercion. Brute force takes what it wants and does not care what the enemy prefers. Coercion depends on his still having a choice. To inflict suffering gains nothing and saves nothing directly, Schelling wrote, it can only make people behave to avoid it. Hence the warning: violence is most purposive and most successful when it is threatened and not used.

The trouble lay in what was done with the theory. The graduated bombing of North Vietnam from 1965 was presented as coercive signalling of exactly this kind, a calibrated sequence of pains meant to bring Hanoi to the table. It did not. Later scholarship, most prominently Robert Pape's work on air power, argues that punishing a population almost never wins the concession sought. Schelling described how coercion works when it works. He was far weaker on how seldom that is.

He had meanwhile become an insider, with an informal line to Henry Kissinger, Nixon's national security adviser and lately a Harvard colleague. At the end of April 1970 American forces invaded Cambodia. Schelling organised about a dozen senior Harvard faculty, decided himself who would see whom, and took them to Washington in May to argue against it.

What he said in Kissinger's office survives only as a Harvard Crimson paraphrase of roughly how it went. As we see it, there are two possibilities. Either the President did not understand, when he went into Cambodia, that he was invading another country. Or he did understand.

The group then told Kissinger they were no longer available to him as private advisers, and Schelling kept to it. He had spent fifteen years arguing that a commitment only works when it cannot be taken back, and he chose to spend his own access that way.

b: Sometime in the 1960s he boarded an aeroplane. One afternoon, settling into an airplane seat, I had nothing to read, he wrote later. So he drew a row of noughts and crosses along the margin, scattered at random, and gave each symbol one modest wish: it wanted at least half of its immediate neighbours to be its own kind. Then he moved the discontented ones along, one at a time.

At home he did it again with pennies out of his son's coin collection. The results astonished me, he wrote. A row that had begun thoroughly mixed sorted itself into long blocks of noughts and long blocks of crosses. Nobody in the model wanted segregation, and every one of them was content in a neighbourhood half unlike itself. Separation was where they ended up all the same, every time.

His colleague Herb Scarf suggested moving into two dimensions, with a checkerboard and empty squares to move into. Schelling drew a board of sixteen squares by sixteen, left about a fifth of the spaces blank, and worked through the moves with coins on a coffee table alongside his twelve year old son. The same thing happened.

He published the work in 1969 and in fuller form in 1971, and built the general argument into Micromotives and Macrobehavior in 1978. The patterns we see in a society are often nobody's preference. They are what individual choices add up to. A very small preference for similar neighbours, aggregated across a city, produces extreme separation that no one ever voted for.

This is the other half of his life's work, and it is really the same half. In bargaining he showed that the constraints you place on yourself decide the outcome. Here he showed that outcomes arrive with nobody's intention behind them at all.
ch.cap: A doodle that changed social science
ch.when: A flight, and a living room, in the 1960s

b: He turned the same eye on himself. He had given up smoking in 1955. In 1958, in a London restaurant, he accepted a cigar, and then spent some fifteen years trying to stop all over again.

The fashionable economics of addiction held that an addict weighs pleasure against pain and rationally chooses to continue. Schelling, who had been there, thought this missed everything. In an essay of 1980 called The Intimate Contest for Self-Command he described the smoker as a rational being at war with himself. One self wants to quit and makes the arrangements. Another turns up at eleven at night and overrules them.

The remedy comes from the Paris corridor and the man with bloodshot eyes. You cannot win by resolve, because resolve belongs to the self that is not in the room when it matters. You win by binding the absent self: throwing the packet away, promising in public, making retreat expensive before you ever want to retreat. He gathered the work into Choice and Consequence in 1984, directed Harvard's institute on smoking behaviour and policy for six years, and left for the University of Maryland in 1990.

In October 2005, aged eighty four, he was woken at seven in the morning by a call from Sweden. The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences was his, shared with Robert Aumann, for enhancing our understanding of conflict and cooperation through game theory. In December he gave his Nobel lecture, An Astonishing Sixty Years, The Legacy of Hiroshima, on the strangest fact of his working life: that after 1945 the weapons were never used again. These weapons are unique, he said, and a large part of their uniqueness derives from their being perceived as unique. A taboo, which is to say a focal point, had held for sixty years.

He died in Bethesda, Maryland, on the thirteenth of December 2016, aged ninety five. His family auctioned the Nobel medal for one hundred and eighty seven thousand dollars and gave the proceeds to the Southern Poverty Law Center. The man who taught the world to tie its own hands had, at the end, nothing much left to untie.

connects: Voss's tactics work on exactly Schelling's ground: the leverage sits in what you are visibly unable to give away, not in what you argue.
Clausewitz made war an instrument of politics, and Schelling finished the thought by treating the threat of force itself as the bargaining.
Both books insist that the pattern you see was produced by the structure of many small decisions rather than by anybody's intention.
note: Dates, posts and publication details follow the standard biographies of Schelling, his Nobel materials and his own books. The aeroplane, the pennies and the checkerboard come from Schelling's own memoir of the episode, and the quotations from An Essay on Bargaining, Arms and Influence and the Nobel lecture are verbatim. His mother's remark, the 1940 spell in Chile and the London cigar of 1958 are recollections from interviews and profiles rather than documents, so treat them as his own version of events. The words spoken in Kissinger's office in May 1970 survive only as a Harvard Crimson paraphrase printed as roughly how it went, not as a transcript, and are given here on that footing.
recall: What did Schelling mean by the threat that leaves something to chance?

It is his answer to threats too terrible to be believed. Rather than promising you will certainly retaliate, you arrange forces and procedures so that a crisis could escalate beyond anyone's control, so the other side is deterred by shared risk instead of by your doubted resolve.
Where did Schelling's students say they would meet a stranger in New York, and why does it matter?

A clear majority chose the information booth at Grand Central Station at noon. No logic made it the right answer, only its obviousness, which is why Schelling called such clues focal points and used them to explain tacit coordination.
How did Schelling first discover his segregation result, and what did he use?

On a flight in the 1960s with nothing to read he drew a row of noughts and crosses, each wanting half its neighbours alike, and shuffled the discontented ones along. He repeated it at home with pennies from his son's coin collection, then, on Herb Scarf's suggestion, on a checkerboard of sixteen squares by sixteen.
What happened between Schelling and Henry Kissinger in May 1970?

After American forces invaded Cambodia, Schelling organised about a dozen senior Harvard faculty and took them to Washington to argue against it. They told Kissinger they were no longer available as private advisers, and Schelling never resumed the role.
When was The Strategy of Conflict published, and what was its quarrel with game theory?

It appeared in 1960, assembled from articles written between 1957 and 1960. Its quarrel was with game theory's focus on zero sum games, since Schelling insisted that real conflicts are mixed motive, where enemies share an interest in avoiding the worst outcome.
recap:
Thomas Schelling was born in Oakland in 1921 into a naval family, kept out of the war by a stomach ulcer, and sent instead to Copenhagen and Paris to help run the Marshall Plan. In those rooms he noticed what became his life's idea. The negotiator who won was usually not the one with the better argument but the one who could not move, because a man whose parliament will never ratify another penny has the advantage over a man free to be generous. Freedom to concede is a liability. In his 1956 essay on bargaining he put it in a picture nobody forgets: a man threatening to stab himself on your porch unless given ten dollars is likelier to get the money if his eyes are bloodshot.

At RAND and then Harvard he turned this into The Strategy of Conflict in 1960, which was less an application of game theory than a quarrel with it. Real conflicts are not zero sum, he said, they are mixed motive: enemies who share an interest in avoiding the worst. That shifts the question from how do I win to how do we reach any outcome at all. From it came focal points, discovered when his students, asked where they would meet a stranger in New York with no way to communicate, mostly chose the information booth at Grand Central at noon. Not the best answer, simply the obvious one, which is the whole point.

Applied to Berlin, where no president would really start a nuclear war over an indefensible city, it produced the threat that leaves something to chance: do not promise to retaliate, arrange matters so events might escape everyone's control. He built that into war games at Camp David from 1961, played with Robert Kennedy. His 1960 article on accidental war sent Stanley Kubrick towards Doctor Strangelove, and the same worry helped push the superpowers onto a direct line in 1963. Arms and Influence in 1966 stated the hard version: the power to hurt is bargaining power, and violence is most successful when threatened and not used. The bombing of Vietnam showed how badly that can be misapplied. In 1970 he spent his own access, leading a dozen Harvard colleagues to tell Kissinger they were finished over Cambodia.

Then a doodle on an aeroplane, finished with pennies on a coffee table, showed that a very small preference for similar neighbours produces extreme segregation nobody chose. He ended by bargaining with himself over cigarettes, and by marvelling, in his Nobel lecture of 2005, at sixty years of nuclear forbearance. Tie your own hands, and you will find you have more power, not less.
stories: The aeroplane with nothing to read

Sometime in the 1960s Schelling settled into a plane seat and found he had nothing to read. So he drew a row of noughts and crosses in the margin and gave each one a modest wish: at least half its neighbours should be its own kind. Then he shuffled the unhappy ones along. With no eraser it was tedious work. At home he ran it again with pennies from his son's coin collection, and the mixed row sorted itself into solid blocks. Nobody in the model wanted segregation. They got it anyway, and a field of social science was born on a tray table.

In September 1960 Schelling published a short piece on accidental war in the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, discussing Peter George's novel Red Alert, in which a general launches his bombers alone. Stanley Kubrick read it. Conversations between Kubrick, Schelling and George followed, and out of them came Doctor Strangelove in 1964. The strategist who spent his life explaining how deterrence holds thus became midwife to the century's great comedy about deterrence failing. It is still the most widely seen piece of strategic theory ever made, which is a thought worth sitting with.

In May 1970, after American forces invaded Cambodia, Schelling gathered about a dozen senior Harvard professors, decided himself which of them would see which official, and took them to Washington. In Henry Kissinger's office, by the Harvard Crimson's account of it, he said that as they saw it there were two possibilities. Either the President had not understood that he was invading another country, or he had. The group then withdrew as Kissinger's private advisers, and Schelling never went back. The man who taught the world about costly commitment paid for his own.
take: Bargaining power is the power to bind yourself
Before any negotiation, decide what you will put beyond your own reach, then say it out loud. A limit the other side can see does more work than an argument they can resist.
Freedom to concede is a liability
If you can always sweeten a deal, the other side will simply wait for it. Give whoever negotiates a mandate they cannot exceed, and make sure the other side knows the mandate exists.
Make a threat credible by sharing the risk, not by raising your voice
A consequence that follows automatically beats one you must choose to impose. Build it into the process so that nobody has to volunteer to be the villain.
People coordinate on what is obvious, not on what is best
When you need concerted action and cannot brief everyone, pick a salient marker: one time, one place, one round number. Obvious beats optimal every time.
Name the interest you share with the other side early and out loud. It moves the question from who wins to how both of you avoid the outcome neither can afford.
The leverage lives in the credible possibility. The moment you use it you have spent it, and usually spent the relationship with it.
Before blaming intent for an outcome, ask what mild individual choices, repeated many times, would produce it. Then change the mechanism rather than lecturing the motives.
Treat your future self as a counterparty
Do not rely on resolve at the moment of temptation, because it will not be there. Remove the option in advance, in public, while you are still the self that wants to.
title: The Man Who Tied His Own Hands
wiifm: You negotiate every day, with lenders, with clients, with staff, and with yourself at eleven at night. This story hands you the one idea most people never learn: that bargaining power comes from what you cannot do, not from what you can. You will come away knowing why a visible constraint persuades better than any argument, why people coordinate on whatever is obvious rather than whatever is best, why a threat you would never carry out can still work if the outcome is partly out of your hands, and why the patterns nobody chose are the hardest ones to shift.
words: Understood or agreed between people without being said out loud.
Schelling's tacit bargaining is how two enemies settle on a limit, such as a river or a weapon left unused, without ever exchanging a word about it.
Standing out so plainly that it is the first thing anyone notices.
A focal point works because it is salient: the information booth at Grand Central was not the best meeting place in New York, only the hardest to overlook.
Deliberately pushing a dangerous situation close to disaster so that the other side gives way.
Schelling redefined brinkmanship as manufacturing a risk you genuinely share, rather than a bluff that can be called.
Impossible to take back, cancel or undo.
A commitment only hands the problem to the other side when it is irrevocable, which is why Schelling thought a burnt bridge was an asset.
Deliberately holding back from doing something you have the power to do.
The sixty years of nuclear forbearance after Hiroshima were, for Schelling, the most astonishing fact of his working life.
